sections.title: Orientation: one organ, three functional regions

nodes.text: A lymph node is a bean-shaped, encapsulated organ positioned along lymphatic vessels. Its supporting stroma and immune cells are organized into a superficial cortex, a deeper paracortex, and a central medulla. Begin with the
whole-organ compartment map
before moving to microscopic detail.
Surface polarity matters.
Numerous afferent lymphatic vessels pierce the convex surface. The opposite concave region is the hilum, where the efferent lymphatic exits and blood vessels enter or leave.
Lymph nodes follow lymphatic vessels throughout the body. Major groups occur in the axilla and groin, along the great vessels of the neck, and within the thorax, abdomen, and mesenteries.

The capsule contains dense connective tissue with collagen, elastin, and fibroblasts. Trabeculae extend inward and continue into a reticular framework rich in type III collagen. This mesh supports lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, antigen-presenting cells, and follicular dendritic cells.

sections.title: Recognizing a lymph node on section

nodes.text: At low power, identify the capsule, a nodule-rich outer cortex, the nodule-free paracortex, and the paler medulla converging toward the hilum. Use the
whole-node section
to rehearse the outside-to-center order.
Trabeculae project from the capsule. Cortical nodules occupy the superficial region, while medullary cords and sinuses form branching networks in the deepest region.

The subcapsular sinus is the first intranodal space entered by afferent lymph. It contains a loose reticular network. Lymph then passes into cortical sinuses, also called intermediate or trabecular sinuses because they follow the trabecular framework.
Primary follicles lack a germinal center. Secondary follicles contain a pale germinal center surrounded by a darker mantle. Compare these landmarks in the
annotated cortex–medulla micrograph

A germinal center contains dark, light, and mantle zones. The dark zone is rich in proliferating centroblasts. In the light zone, centrocytes interact with follicular dendritic cells displaying intact antigen; high-affinity cells persist while weak binders undergo apoptosis.

Macrophages clear apoptotic B cells, while helper T cells support selection and maturation. Surviving B cells can become antibody-secreting plasma cells, memory B cells, or re-enter the circulation. Inspect the
secondary follicle
and distinguish its pale center from the mantle.

sections.title: Paracortex: T cells and high endothelial venules

nodes.text: The paracortex lies between outer cortex and medulla. Its defining pattern is abundant T lymphocytes with no lymphoid nodules. High endothelial venules have cuboidal endothelial cells and provide the major route by which circulating lymphocytes enter the node from blood.

The medulla contains cellular medullary cords separated by medullary sinuses. Cords contain lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, and reticular cells. Sinuses provide channels for lymph approaching the hilum and are traversed by a reticular mesh that supports filtration.

Valved afferent vessels deliver lymph to the subcapsular sinus. Flow continues through cortical or trabecular sinuses, then through medullary sinuses, and finally leaves through an efferent lymphatic at the hilum. Follow the complete route in the
hilar circulation image
Source correction:
the final source slide incorrectly states that lymph leaves through afferent vessels. Its diagram and the preceding sequence establish that lymph exits through the efferent vessel.
